name: 4-Androstenediol (4-AD)

lead: 4-Androstenediol (4-AD) is a steroid closely related to testosterone that was sold as an oral supplement in the 2000s. It was marketed to raise testosterone and build muscle.

It is described as converting to testosterone in the body at a low rate, and some of the resulting testosterone can convert to estrogen. Rat testis tissue can make the conversion in vitro, and the compound has been studied mainly for doping detection. A review of the wider prohormone class concluded that marketing claims for testosterone, strength and muscle gains had not been well supported by controlled human studies. No trial of it for physique goals was found.

paras: It was taken orally as a supplement in the early 2000s, typically as part of bodybuilding stacks of the prohormone era.
Reviews of oral andro prohormones raised health concerns, and related 19-nor prohormones are on the WADA prohibited list. Specific legal status was not documented.

angle.text: 4-AD was sold as a prohormone that converts to testosterone, raising androgen signalling to support more muscle. A review of the prohormone class found its marketing claims had not been well supported by controlled human studies.

lead: 4-Androstenediol (androst-4-ene-3β,17β-diol, also written 4-AD, 4-diol or 4-ADIOL) is a steroid related to testosterone that was sold in the early 2000s as an oral "prohormone" supplement.[1] Lifters took it to raise testosterone, which they hoped would bring more muscle, less body fat and a fuller, harder-looking physique.[2]

Chemically it is an androgen that the body converts to testosterone, at a reported rate of about 16 percent, roughly three times that of androstenedione because a different enzyme route is involved.[1] Rat testis tissue was shown to make this conversion in laboratory work published in 1966,[3] and the compound has since been studied mainly in doping control, where urinary markers were developed to detect its use in athletes.[4] A 2003 review of the oral andro prohormone class reported that most controlled studies did not support manufacturers' claims of higher testosterone, strength and muscle mass.[2]

The Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004 placed 4-androstenediol and other prohormones in US Schedule III, ending their sale as over-the-counter supplements; the law took effect on 20 January 2005.[5] Today the compound is mainly of historical interest in bodybuilding and supplement history.
infobox: 1999 patent held by Patrick Arnold for raising testosterone[1]
Controlled prohormone under the 2004 Anabolic Steroid Control Act (Schedule III)[5]

paras: 4-Androstenediol is one of several androstenediol isomers. The 4-ene form is structurally closer to testosterone than 5-androstenediol is.[1] It was sold in capsule and tablet products, often next to androstenedione and 19-nor analogues, in a wave of "andro" supplements aimed at gym-goers and bodybuilders.[2]

Prohormones in general are weakly active or inactive precursors that the body converts into an active hormone. The most common supplement prohormones are synthetic anabolic steroid precursors marketed for muscle growth, and many were sold with little regulation before legal restrictions arrived.

The attraction for lifters was physique-related: higher testosterone is associated with greater muscle protein synthesis and lower fat mass, so a compound that raised it was marketed as a shortcut to size and leanness.[2] Claims of the period included higher serum testosterone, greater strength and muscle mass, reduced body fat, better mood and improved sexual performance.[2]
Because it was sold as a dietary supplement rather than a drug, it was available without a prescription in the United States until federal rules changed in the mid-2000s.[5]

Wikipedia reports that 4-androstenediol is a weak partial agonist of the androgen receptor that can behave like an antiandrogen when full agonists such as testosterone or dihydrotestosterone are present, and that it is only very weakly estrogenic, at about half a percent of estradiol's affinity for the estrogen receptors.[1] Some of the testosterone it yields is in turn converted to estrogens.[1]

A 1966 in vitro study found that rat testis tissue converted both 4-androstenediol and 5-androstenediol to testosterone, and converted dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) to 4-androstenediol.[3] A pharmacological study of 4-androstenediol derivatives was published as early as 1946.[6]
No studies found of 4-androstenediol itself for muscle, strength or body composition in humans.

The closest human research is a 2003 review of the oral andro prohormone class, which covered androstenedione, 4-androstenediol, 5-androstenediol, 19-norandrostenediol and 19-norandrostenedione. Its authors reported that most studies up to then contradicted claims of increased serum testosterone, strength and muscle mass.[2] It also noted that several studies of oral andro prohormones found abnormal elevations in estrogen-related hormones and significant declines in HDL cholesterol.[2] Separate forensic work describes urinary markers for detecting 4-androstenediol administration in athletes.[4]

5-Androstenediol (also called androstenediol or A5) is a naturally occurring steroid and an intermediate in the conversion of DHEA to testosterone. Wikipedia reports that it is far less androgenic than testosterone in rats and has estrogenic activity, with about 6 percent of estradiol's affinity for estrogen receptor alpha and 17 percent for beta, and that it circulates at much higher concentrations than estradiol [7].

Separately, 5-androstenediol was studied by the US Armed Forces Radiobiology Research Institute as a radiation countermeasure, under the proposed name Neumune, mainly for effects on white blood cells and platelets; in a rhesus monkey study 12.5 percent of 40 treated animals died versus 32.5 percent on placebo, and a federal biodefense request for such products was cancelled in 2007 [7]. This is research on the 5-ene isomer rather than on 4-androstenediol.

19-Nor-4-androstenediol is a related prohormone of nandrolone that appears on the WADA prohibited list; a 2008 rat study reported that a related 19-nor steroid increased muscle mass and bone mineral density relative to prostate mass [8][9].

The 2003 review raised concerns about long-term oral use, in particular effects on blood lipids and on estrogen levels, and linked abnormal estrogen elevations to possible prostate and pancreatic risk.[2] Because supplement products of the period varied in content, the effects of any given product could differ from those of the pure compound.[5]

Prohormones including 4-androstenediol were named in the Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004, signed on 22 October 2004 and effective 20 January 2005, which listed them in Schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act.[5] The same law's definition, built around effects on testosterone, led manufacturers to turn to compounds that did not obviously fall under it, sometimes called designer steroids.[5] Related 19-nor prohormones were the subject of doping-control research because their metabolites overlap with nandrolone markers.[10]

A pharmacological study of 4-androstenediol derivatives appeared in 1946,[6] and in vitro testis conversion work in 1966.[3] In 1999 Patrick Arnold was granted a patent on using 4-androstenediol to raise testosterone in humans,[1] and products entered the supplement market in the years that followed. US federal control arrived with the 2004 act.[5]
